formulaCard.title: Randomized Comparative Experiment

explanation: A [[kw:controlled experiment]] has two groups studied under identical conditions except for one variable.
The [[kw:control group]] receives no treatment (or a placebo) and serves as a baseline.
The [[kw:treatment group]] receives the treatment being tested.
[[kw:Randomization]] is the process of randomly assigning subjects to groups. This minimizes bias and makes groups similar in all ways before treatment.
A [[kw:randomized comparative experiment]] is a controlled experiment where subjects are randomly assigned to control or treatment groups.
A [[kw:placebo]] is a harmless, fake treatment that looks like the real one, used to prevent psychological effects from influencing results.

examples.prompt: A study gave vitamin C to 50 patients who chose to take it, and monitored 50 who chose not to. Cholesterol was 15% lower in the vitamin C group. Is this a randomized comparative experiment?
steps: The patients chose their own group – no random assignment.
This is not a randomized comparative experiment.
Other factors (diet, exercise) could explain the lower cholesterol.
The conclusion that vitamin C lowers cholesterol may not be valid.

discoveryHook.scenario: You read that people who drink green tea live longer. Does green tea cause longer life, or do health‑conscious people just tend to drink it? Only an experiment – randomly assigning people to drink tea or not – could prove causation, but that might be impractical. That's when an observational study is used instead.

explanation: An [[kw:experiment]] randomly assigns subjects to treatments. It can establish cause and effect.
An [[kw:observational study]] observes subjects without imposing a treatment. It can identify correlations, but not prove causation.
[[imp:Only a well‑designed randomized experiment can show causality.]] Observational studies may have confounding variables.
Ethics often dictate the method: we can't force people to smoke or assign them to unhealthy behaviors.
In an observational study, random sampling from the groups of interest can still produce useful comparisons, but we must be cautious about conclusions.

formulaCard.title: Causality vs. Correlation
notes: Causation: one variable directly affects the other.

examples.prompt: You want to know whether vigorous exercise in older people leads to longer life. Experiment or observational study?
steps: We cannot force some elderly people to exercise vigorously and others not — it's unethical.
So we must use an observational study.
We would identify a group who already exercises vigorously and a group who doesn't, and follow them over time.
We can find correlation, but not definite causation, because other factors (diet, genetics) may differ.
examples.title: Example A – Choose the Method

examples.prompt: You want to know whether spraying flowers with water twice a day keeps them fresh longer. Experiment or observational study? Design it.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why is an experiment possible here? How would you randomly assign flowers? What would the control group be?
steps: An experiment is possible — we can control the treatment.
Obtain a large number of similar flowers. Randomly assign half to be sprayed (treatment) and half not (control).
Keep all other conditions identical (light, temperature).
Measure freshness over time. Because we randomly assigned, we can conclude causation if there's a difference.
examples.title: Example B – Flower Mist Experiment

examples.prompt: A study monitored driving records of 140 early risers and 140 non‑early risers. The early risers had 12% fewer accidents. Is this an experiment or observational study? Can it prove waking up early causes better driving?
examples.title: Example C – Identify the Study Type
steps: This is an observational study — people already were early risers or not; no treatment was assigned.
It shows correlation (early risers had fewer accidents) but cannot prove causation.
Other factors (e.g., early risers may drive less at night, be more alert) could explain the difference.

confusionCorner.body: Just because two things happen together doesn't mean one causes the other. Ice cream sales and drowning both increase in summer — they're correlated, but ice cream doesn't cause drowning. (The hidden variable is hot weather.)

examples.title: Example A – Small Sample Problem
examples.prompt: A gum company tests weight‑loss gum on 10 people (5 gum, 5 placebo). After 3 months, the gum group lost weight. What's wrong?

steps: Groups are not similar — gender is completely confounded with treatment.
We can't tell if the difference is due to gum or gender.
Fix: Use a randomized block design — split by gender, then randomly assign gum/placebo within each gender group.
Then compare gum vs. placebo within each gender.

Improvement: randomly assign 100 to supplement and 100 to placebo, and compare.

discoveryHook.scenario: A company tests a new weight‑loss gum on only 10 people and claims it works. Would you trust that? Probably not — the sample was tiny, and we don't know if it was compared to a control group. Good experimental design requires a large sample, random assignment, a control group, and replication.

formulaCard.title: Experimental Design Checklist
notes: All four elements strengthen the conclusions.
Lack of any one weakens the validity.

rows.1: Large enough to detect an effect
Subjects grouped by key variable, then randomized

explanation: [[kw:Sample size]] is the number of subjects in an experiment. Larger samples give more reliable results and reduce the effect of chance.
[[kw:Replication]] means repeating the experiment under the same or similar conditions. It confirms that results are not just a fluke.
[[kw:Control group]] is essential for comparison. Without it, you can't tell if the treatment had any effect beyond natural changes.
[[kw:Randomization]] ensures groups are similar before treatment, eliminating confounding variables.
A [[kw:randomized block design]] groups subjects by a characteristic (like age or gender) and then randomly assigns within each block. This controls for that characteristic's effect.

confusionCorner.title: Random Assignment vs. Random Sampling
confusionCorner.body: Random sampling (from a population) helps generalize results. Random assignment (to groups) eliminates bias within the experiment. A study can have one without the other.

blocks.title: Evaluating Published Experiments

discoveryHook.scenario: Headlines often scream 'New study proves chocolate helps you lose weight!' But before you stock up, ask: Was it a randomized experiment? How large was the sample? Was there a control group? Evaluating studies critically separates real science from hype.

formulaCard.title: Study Evaluation Checklist
notes: The more criteria a study meets, the more trustworthy its conclusions.
Observational studies can be valuable but should be interpreted cautiously.

explanation: To evaluate a study's validity, ask these questions:
1. Was it a [[imp:randomized comparative experiment]]? If subjects were not randomly assigned, it's observational.
2. Was there a [[imp:control group]]? Without it, you can't gauge the treatment's effect.
3. Was the [[imp:sample size]] large enough? Small samples may produce results by chance.
4. Was it [[imp:replicated]]? A single study is never definitive.
5. Could [[imp:confounding variables]] explain the result? Other differences between groups may be the real cause.

rows.1: Groups differ in other important ways (age, gender, lifestyle)

confusionCorner.body: Always consider whether it's ethical to withhold a potentially beneficial treatment from the control group, or to expose the treatment group to possible harm. Sometimes an observational study is the only ethical choice.

formulaCard.title: Blueprint Formula for Valid Experiment
notes: Always compare at least two groups (treatment vs. control).
Replication confirms results are not due to chance.

rows.1: State hypothesis, define treatment and outcome variable.
Choose sample size, random assignment method, control group.
Ensure identical conditions except for the treatment.
Run experiment, gather data, compare groups.

explanation: 1. [[imp:Understand]] – State the hypothesis. What is the treatment? What is the outcome you'll measure? Define the population.
2. [[imp:Plan]] – Decide sample size. Plan random assignment to treatment and control groups. Use blocking if needed. Prepare a placebo if applicable.
3. [[imp:Control]] – Keep all other conditions identical between groups (environment, timing, measurement).
4. [[imp:Collect & Compare]] – Run the experiment, collect data, and compare results. Use appropriate statistical methods.
5. [[imp:Conclude & Replicate]] – Determine if the difference is significant. Replicate the experiment to confirm findings.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Designing an Experiment

examples.prompt: Design an experiment to test whether playing classical music helps plants grow taller.
examples.title: Example A – Music and Plant Growth
steps: Understand: Hypothesis – classical music increases growth. Treatment = music. Outcome = height increase.
Plan: Obtain 60 similar plants. Randomly assign 30 to 'music' group (play classical music daily) and 30 to control (no music).
Control: Same light, water, temperature, pots, soil for all plants. Same schedule except music.
Collect & Compare: Measure heights weekly for 6 weeks. Compare average growth.
Conclude & Replicate: If music group grows significantly more, experiment should be repeated with different plants.

examples.title: Example B – Fixing a Flawed Design
steps: Flaw: Gender is completely tied to treatment – males got drink, females placebo. We can't separate gender from drink effect.
Redesign: Recruit equal numbers of male and female athletes. Within each gender, randomly assign half to energy drink and half to placebo.
Now we can compare drink vs. placebo within each gender, and also see if gender matters.
